However, I, Krsysl Wordsmith, do not wish to wait for the dust to have metaphorically settled.
Krsysl Wordsmith’s works have never been—how shall I put it?—particularly innovative.

He nodded to a man hunched over in his chair in the corner of the room. The [Writer] didn’t respond, only grunted as his quill darted across the paper he was writing on.
Andel, the [Writer] who’d been hunched over his work looked up and made a sound.
Jasi sat up and looked at Andel. The [Writer] solemnly blew on the paper he’d been writing on and looked up.
The [Writer] sat back, gulping from his mug of ale. He collected the pages, delicately filing them flat against the table, then handed them to Wesle.
The [Writer] pursed his lips.
She hesitated, about to reprimand the [Writer], but Pralcem spoke up impatiently.
The [Writer] permitted himself a smile, relieved and proud at the same time.
The half-strangled shriek came from the [Writer]. Andel’s face was purpling, and he looked as though he might pass out.
Jasi bristled, but Wesle slapped a hand over Andel’s mouth. The [Writer] struggled, but both Wesle and Kilkran held him back.
“Orica!”
“Yes. Put aside all your projects for now, Orica. We want you to rewrite Macbeth.”
Andel hurried over.
